variants.name: tower Service/Layer middleware stack
variants.idiom_name: Service<Request> wrapped by Layer, composed with ServiceBuilder
variants.implementation_notes: Rust has no inheritance, so the ecosystem standardises the chain in tower: a `Service` is an async function from request to response, a `Layer` wraps one service in another (timeout, retry, load-shedding, rate limiting), and `ServiceBuilder` composes layers so the first added is the outermost. The wrapped service is the successor and the user's service is the terminal; the pass-or-stop reading appears as a layer that returns early with an error instead of calling `inner.call(req)`. Use this variant whenever the stack already depends on hyper, tonic or axum.
pitfalls: Service::call takes &mut self, so a stack is usually cloned per request; a non-cloneable handler forces Arc<Mutex<_>> and contention.
ServiceBuilder order is outermost-first while the type nest grows inside-out, so verify order in a test rather than by reading the builder chain.
Discarding an error with a bare ? conflates 'rejected by this layer' with 'failed downstream', which changes what later layers observe.

variants.name: Box<dyn Handler> successor chain (framework-free)
variants.idiom_name: trait Handler { fn handle(&mut self, req: &Request) -> Option<Response>; } with Option<Box<dyn Handler>>
variants.implementation_notes: Without tower the classic structure is expressed with trait objects: a `Handler` trait whose `handle` returns an optional response (None meaning 'not handled') and an `Option<Box<dyn Handler>>` successor. Ownership replaces pointers - Box gives the chain sole ownership and &mut self preserves per-handler state - and the Rust book documents trait objects as the sanctioned way to allow heterogeneous implementations behind one interface, which is exactly the role Handler plays. Prefer an enum when the handler set is closed.
pitfalls: An enum-based chain is usually better than Box<dyn Handler> for a closed set of handlers: no dynamic dispatch and exhaustiveness checking for free.
Recursive trait objects need indirection (Box or &mut dyn) or the compiler rejects the type as infinitely sized.
Sharing the chain across threads requires Send + Sync bounds on the trait object; without them it cannot be moved into a task.
